Reading this beautifully observed description of two sessions with ‘Max’, in which the Goal-Based Outcomes Measure (GBOM, Law, 2009) is used to set and then review three treatment goals, two questions spring to mind. First, would one want to involve Max’s parents in this process? Second, does Max’s behaviour in the second reported session, so different from his rating of the goals, completely belie that rating and, if so, does it invalidate the exercise?

The question of involving parents in goal-setting is a complex one (Emanuel et al., 2013) and, of course, the therapist may well have been influenced by usual practice in his or her CAMHS. For Max’s parents, being asked to set goals, or rate Max’s, might have been difficult given their struggle with taking on the emotional impact of his disability on him. In this extract we are told about Max and his family. Max has hemiplegic cerebral palsy and has been having ‘aggressive outbursts in which he physically attacked his mother and destroyed his own valued objects.’ Max’s parents are seeking help, but when asked why Max might be so distraught they express that they recognise Max ‘was in great distress but could genuinely think of nothing that he might be distressed about.’

This background context to the individual psychotherapy sessions very helpfully illuminates what follows.

As a reader, the cause for Max’s distress seems immediately apparent and jumps out of the page. We see a boy consistently trying to communicate to the adults around him a sense of what it’s like to live with cerebral palsy. Interestingly, what appears so immediately to the reader, in the position of ‘outsider looking in’, does not appear to be recognised by the key players in the drama, Max’s parents. There seems to be a ‘blind spot’ for his parents, as if they need to maintain a stance of ‘determined positivity’ in the face of Max’s disability. This position does not appear to leave space for any of the family to express more ambivalent expressions of regret, disappointment, anger or loss. This collective ‘blind spot’ is fascinating and suggests a powerful unconscious group dynamic in process. It is this dynamic that I wish to focus on below, to illustrate how the therapist and the application of the outcome measurements appear to get caught up in this dynamic too.

In their assessment, the clinicians thoughtfully insist that fortnightly parallel work with the parents should take place ‘to help them explore and tolerate the reality of their son’s emotional life, including the ongoing loss and pain of having the bad luck to be born with an impairment of this kind, and the anxiety of not knowing how disabled he might be as an adult.’ The dilemma for Max’s family is clearly stated along with an implicit idea that unless Max’s parents can tolerate and express all their thoughts and feelings about Max’s disability – both positive and negative – then they are unlikely to be able to help their son come to terms with his feelings. Otherwise Max and his parents seem destined to remain unable to ‘unlock the puzzle’ of his unhappiness.

Teresa Bailey and Kate Stratton

Kate Stratton

Kate Stratton  

Catalina Bronstein’s article discusses the symbolic function of physical symptoms, in this case, eczema and asthma, and the meaning of their appearance in the transference. This moving article explores the connection between the development of severe eczema and asthma in an eight-year-old girl and her problems experiencing mental pain and conflict. She examines the transference around the child’s psychosomatic reaction in therapy sessions. Bronstein’s detailed attention to this girl leads her to suggest that this case may explain why some patients, despite experiencing intense physical sensations, can seem flat and emotionally ‘hollow’. She thinks that these children have a sense of emptiness as a result of the need for very early dissociation because of fear of annihilation, fear that is experienced in the body. Based on her observations in this case, Bronstein believes that a sudden psychosomatic symptom in a session may be the result of intense hostility towards the object. However, this arouses terror, as the hated object is also the loved object and essential for the child’s survival. She thinks that the therapist may unwittingly help trigger such an episode by not containing the child’s projections leading to the patient feeling she has to take back raw ‘psycho-physical’ emotions. This article discusses the different degrees – and forms – of symbolic functioning in connection to this girl’s experience of her eczema and asthma and their manifestation in the transference relationship to the therapist.

The complexity of clinical work with children who display challenging and violent behaviour is the subject of the next article by Peter Slater. Drawing on his doctoral research study, based on three-times-weekly psychotherapy with a boy who had witnessed domestic violence, the author vividly conveys the many challenges of understanding and working clinically with such a child. Slater describes how his research design, which was based on grounded theory and rooted in psychoanalytic ideas about the role and function of violence, allowed four clinical concepts – space, time, temperature and distance – to emerge. These, he argues, provide a framework for the therapist and take on a particular importance when working therapeutically with a violent child. One particularly interesting aspect of the article is the exploration of the management of violent behaviours in the therapeutic setting. As he traces his work with ‘Cory’, Slater highlights the ‘paradoxical situation’ faced by the therapist who needs to allow the patient’s violent behaviour to enter the therapy room while remaining alert to the risk that this same violence could lead to the destruction of the therapeutic setting. The clinical material is rich and detailed as we follow Slater’s all-too-understandable efforts to manage his patient’s and his own powerful feelings.

It must be terrible for parents like Lizzie’s, to ‘watch powerless’ as their ordinary 18-month-old toddler goes into a devastating developmental reverse such as this. We learn that both her parents and professionals wonder whether her (apparently) chronic and severely painful digestive problems and food allergies, which lead to serious skin reactions, have played a significant part in Lizzie’s shut down. Physically, both internally in her stomach and bowels, and externally on the surface of her body through her skin, she has been suffering chronic pain. So this certainly seems to be a wise hypothesis about a possible cause of her drastic emotional withdrawal. Research digest: trauma, maltreatment and the needs of children in the care system

Psychopathology among youths who were victims of documented childhood maltreatment

Ricardo J. Pinto & Ângela C. Maia

Child and Adolescent Mental Health, Wiley, 2014, Volume 19 (2): 122–30

Background: There is an established relationship between childhood maltreatment and later psychopathology, but most studies have used self-reports and only consider a small number of experiences. The main aim of this study was to examine predictors of psychopathology by comparing two sources (official records vs. self-reports) of ten different childhood adversities among youths who were identified by Child Protective Services (CPS). We also used a comparison group that was not identified by CPS. This study also compared, in terms of psychopathology, three groups of respondents (under-report; agreement and over-report) based on the discrepancy between the two sources of childhood adversity. Method: The sample included 136 youths, ages 14–23 years, identified by CPS prior to age 12 as being maltreated and who lived with their family for at least five years. The comparison group included 80 youths. Results: The identified youths were not different from the comparison group in global psychopathology. Psychopathology was associated only with the total amount of self-reported adverse experiences, with depressive symptoms being predicted by both documented and self-reported sexual abuse. Females reported and had more documented adversities, presenting an increased risk for psychopathology. The under-report group had a higher mean of documented experiences and a lower mean in psychopathology. Conclusions: Despite the limitations of a self-report methodology, our findings attest to its contribution in predicting health outcomes. Professionals from CPS need to be thorough when assessing and documenting the multiple experiences that may co-occur in a household, paying particular attention when young girls are involved, as the experience of sexual abuse has been shown to be independently associated with later risk of developing depressive symptoms. This process may increase the appropriateness of the chosen interventions.

Teresa Bailey and Kate Stratton

Kate Stratton  

This general edition of the Journal has an apparent mix of themes but there are developmental links between them along the lines of communication, attachment, loss and the retrieval of the good object.

In the first paper, Elena Molinari examines the processing and containing of emotions and sensations in work with autistic children. She hypothesises that babies develop the means to process experience via containment: proto-containment – the sensory, imitative aspect of the earliest relationship – and containment which propels their emotions towards something meaningful (♀/♂) through the α function, projection and introjection. Molinari’s hypothesis is that the autistic child is unable to move between these two forms of containment. She uses a clinical case to explore this hypothesis, examining the therapeutic process and the countertransference of the therapist. She describes how, through this work, she came to understand that the development of introjective and projective functions is core for the development of the psychic container. Molinari compares the way in which the communication of feelings through action in therapy can ‘cross the void’ in a way similar to what happens in an artistic performance.

The next article provides an example of a piece of research with real practical application. Carol Broughton’s paper succinctly explains the genesis, construction and preliminary reliability testing of the Parent–Infant Relational Assessment Tool (PIRAT), a clinical measure, predicated on psychoanalytic understanding, attachment theory and clinical research, designed to identify risk in the early parent–infant relationship. Broughton outlines the beginnings of the assessment tool in the Parent Infant Project at the Anna Freud Centre in 1997 where the need was identified for a flexible, reliable and validated measure to facilitate the transfer of knowledge about infant research and to allow health professionals to identify and highlight areas of concern about parent–infant dyads. The article also provides an account of the process of training a panel of ten professionals – midwives, health visitors, social workers and clinical psychologists – using videotaped recordings of their own consultations with mothers and their infants. Of particular interest are the verbatim extracts from the participants’ discussions about interactions they were struggling to code and their reflections, on completing the training, on how they felt it had enhanced their practice: as one participant put it, PIRAT provided them with ‘a language to use amongst us – a common language in relation to parents and infants’.

Clinical material

Background

Rebecca was referred to her local CAMHS service at the age of seven presenting with selective mutism. Her parents had split up with some acrimony when she was just three years old. She stopped talking to her father, who moved out and, almost at once, started a new relationship and a new family. She now sees her father only irregularly and has remained mute in his care, though she will speak to her new baby half-sister. Rebecca had never spoken at nursery or school, managing by smiling, nodding and following what the other children did. Her teachers report now that she is bright but immensely shy in class, showing greater social engagement in the playground as long as she does not perceive herself to be observed. However, she had continued to speak at home with her mother and two older siblings until, between the referral to ourselves and Rebecca attending the clinic, she stopped talking with mother altogether after a trip to the dentist for a check-up. In parallel parent sessions, it has become clear that Rebecca’s mother finds it difficult to either reflect on the dynamics between them or to stick to boundaries when parenting Rebecca. She expresses quiet distress that her daughter has stopped talking with her but this takes the form of a feeling of deep personal hurt and rejection. She now tends to ‘walk on eggshells’ around Rebecca, going to great lengths to organise alternative ways for Rebecca to communicate at home such as gestural signing or writing in a special notebook – all of which Rebecca robustly ignores.

Session

Prior to each session, I wonder if Rebecca will be able to stay in the room without her mother and how her mother may facilitate or hinder their separation. If mother does not bring Rebecca in, she will cling aggressively to her leg and refuse to come in at all. Although we have been working on mother being able to leave the room over several weeks – and have settled on aiming for a ‘simple goodbye’ – their parting still always feels touch and go. I expect it to take a while at the beginning of each session for Rebecca to warm to me enough to engage and yet there is usually meaningful contact once she settles in.

Eve Ashley   *Corresponding Author. Email: Eve.Ashley@sussexpartnership.nhs.uk

Clinical commentary by Eve Ashley, child and adolescent psychotherapist and psychoanalytic couple psychotherapist

We all practise selective mutism in some sense, in that none of us has the ability, or choice, to say everything that is on our minds. There is a constant editing process occurring that is specific to each person and place. We use the phrase ‘selective mutism’ to suggest that someone is choosing not to respond verbally in a way that they have previously been quite capable of doing. Selective mutism presents the interlocking puzzles of why is the person not talking and to whom is the person not talking.

Although silence might initially present as a benign form of resistance, the person who remains silent with others where once there was free flowing communication, can create huge feelings of resentment and hostility.

In this child’s background there is a powerful question mark over her parents’ separation. We might wonder what their relationship was like before and after the separation and how it is now, four years on, four years in which Rebecca has grown from a three-year-old to a school child of seven, during which she has not spoken openly at nursery or school. When she sees her father, she doesn’t speak to him either, but just to her baby half-sister. Further silence has grown recently between Rebecca and her mother since a visit to the dentist for a check-up.

There seems to be a link between what she will let out of her mouth and what she fears will be put in her mouth. One of the roles of a therapist is to enable the unspoken and the unheard to have an existence in the world. The carefully framed interpretation, the capacity to hold a helpful silence and the ability to know how to use our eyes, are all therapeutic skills that contribute to the birth of shared thoughts.

The beginning of the session enables a sensitive exploration of her anxieties around separation, particularly from her mother, before the sessions. It feels as though their actual separation process has not sufficiently developed into Rebecca being able to let go of her mother and neither is she confident of meeting up again with her mother after separation. Her behaviour is described as either aggressively clinging to mum’s leg, or seemingly being abruptly brushed off by mum, after which she has a ‘deflated feel’. Her deflation seems to highlight a loss of the connection and ongoing development of relationship between mum and herself. It is likely that mum felt overwhelmed when the separation from Rebecca’s father occurred and had little stability left over to offer her children and Rebecca’s mutism begins at the same time as the separation. Rebecca keeping her coat on when mum leaves reflects her need to keep herself together; she needs the extra skin (Bick, 1987) to cope with being in the session and losing mum. At this point, it hardly seems surprising that she also keeps her mouth shut too.

The impact of mentalization training on the reflective function of novice therapists: a randomized controlled trial

Karen Ensink, Julie Maheux, Lina Normandin, Stéphane Sabourin, Louis Diguer, Nicolas Berthelot and Kathy Parent

Psychotherapy Research, Taylor & Francis, 2013, Volume 23 (5): 526–38

This study examined whether training can increase the reflective function (RF) of novice therapists with patients with Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD). A total of 48 students in clinical psychology were randomly assigned to mentalization training or didactic training. Their RF regarding patients was assessed with the Therapist Mental Activity Scale (TMAS: Normandin, Ensink, & Maheux, 2012). The RF of trainees assigned to the mentalization training improved significantly, while participants who received traditional didactic training actually became significantly less reflective. These findings show that brief mentalization training can help beginner therapists develop their mentalization capacities with challenging patients.

Mind-mindedness and theory of mind: mediating roles of language and perspectival symbolic play

Elizabeth Meins, Charles Fernyhough, Bronia Arnott, Susan R. Leekam and Marc de Rosnay

Child Development, Wiley, 2013, Volume 84 (5): 1777–90

Relations among indices of maternal mind-mindedness (appropriate and non-attuned mind-related comments) and children’s: (a) internal state vocabulary and perspectival symbolic play at 26 months (N = 206) and (b) theory of mind (ToM) at 51 months (n = 161) were investigated. Appropriate comments were positively associated with ToM, but were unrelated to internal state language and perspectival symbolic play. Non-attuned comments were negatively correlated with internal state language and perspectival symbolic play, but were unrelated to ToM. Path analyses indicated that the best fit model assumed: (a) indirect links between non-attuned comments and ToM via children’s perspectival symbolic play, (b) a direct link between appropriate comments and ToM, and (c) an indirect link between appropriate comments and ToM via children’s concurrent receptive verbal ability.

Thinking space: promoting thinking about race, culture and diversity in psychotherapy and beyond

Robert Fleming

Robert Fleming

London
SE11 6JJ
UK

Robert Fleming   *Email: Robert.fleming@slam.nhs.uk

This is an important and timely book. As our society slowly emerges from the worst recession since the Second World War, the re-structuring of the economy seems to have inequality as a central feature (Dransfield, 2014). Environments of huge disparity are often the breeding ground for racism.

Frank Lowe has been facilitating a ‘thinking space’ in the form of a regular discussion forum at the Tavistock since 2002 and this book brings together some of the important presentations that promote thinking about race, culture and diversity in psychotherapy. It challenges the comfortable status quo of the psychoanalytic world and asks the reader actually to think. It goads us to resist remaining silent. It asks us to not circumvent some of the pressing issues facing us all today.

The central tenets of the book are that we all internalise to some extent the hatred that is part of our culture (for example, racism and sexism). Lowe suggests that we all use splitting and projection with each other in order to feel better about ourselves. He argues that the powerful in society dehumanise the weak by stressing difference (for example, race and class). ‘What is hated in the different other is what is feared in the self’ (p. 8).

In eleven chapters, Lowe as editor brings together articles that are broadly psychoanalytic but are also coherently multi-theoretical and stimulating. From the start of the book Lowe points out that despite some improvements, there is a lack of regular thinking space about diversity in most psychotherapy trainings. His first chapter starts with Klein and Bion and convincingly argues that we must become aware of our own capacity for destruction in order to resist causing unnecessary suffering to others. Lowe asserts that we all have a capacity to use others for our own benefit and to understand this is to start better to understand racism.

Onel Brooks argues that we might not be properly thinking about crucial issues like race as a result of our own identifications and idealisations. In a chapter that references Wittgenstein, Brooks claims that what passes for thinking in psychoanalysis is often a ‘matter of saying what those in one’s group tend to say’ (p. 39). Self-love or narcissism allows us to decline the invitation properly to think about difficult issues like race.

Lida Anagnostaki

Lida Anagnostaki   *Email: lidaanagnostaki@hotmail.com

I feel honoured to comment on such rich and thought-provoking material from a session with a seven-year-old girl, Rebecca, with selective mutism. It might feel ironic for a ‘talking cure’, but silence in the therapy room may be polymorphous, meaningful, 305 productive and even valuable (Akhtar, 2013). Whenever I think of selective mutism, however, a well-known Homeric phrase comes to my mind, words uttered by Zeus, father of the gods, when his daughter Athena accused him of having abandoned Ulysses: “My child, what words have escaped the fence of your teeth?” (Homer, 1992, The Odyssey, Rhapsody A:64). Imagine my surprise when I read that Rebecca stopped talking to her mother after a trip to the dentist! Did she get scared that the ‘fence of her teeth’ would be intruded upon? That the presumably very angry words she withholds would ‘escape’ from her, and her aggression would be out in the open, destroying everything, her abandoning parents and omnipotent self included?

The silence of patients with selective mutism is highly overdetermined: unconscious meaning is attached to it. The act of speaking becomes dangerous, as the child equates it to an act of aggression. Silence, then, becomes the child’s way of defending against the forbidden impulse. At the same time, however, silence can become very hostile, as it is used as a punishment and a weapon against the parents who want their child to speak (Yanof, 1996). It seems that Rebecca’s mother has fallen victim to her daughter’s ‘silent’ aggression: she tries hard to organise ways for Rebecca to communicate, which Rebecca quite sadistically ignores. On the other hand, the mother seems unconsciously to feel her daughter’s deeply rooted aggression toward her: she ‘walks on eggshells’ around her, while she feels personally hurt and rejected.

So what about the therapist? ‘How can such silence be therapeutically approached? It risks being overrun by our verbiage, just as its meanings may be subtly consumed by our anxious efforts to aid and explain and encode’ (Youngerman, 1979: 283). Getting comfortable in an endlessly silent room, enduring the uncertainties, doubts and mysteries that the silence only make greater, is the therapist’s task of ‘negative capability’ (Keats, 1899: 277). Admittedly, it is not an easy one.

Research on the couch: single-case studies, subjectivity and scientific knowledge

Michael Rustin

Michael Rustin

London
UK

Michael Rustin   *Email: m.j.rustin@uel.ac.uk

Robert Hinshelwood’s new book is a valuable contribution to the debates concerning the scientific status of psychoanalysis and about how psychoanalytic theories can find a rational justification. Hinshelwood’s primary interest is in the validity of psychoanalytic theories of the mind, not in the ‘evidence-based’ measures of treatment outcome, which now receive most attention. He has concerns about the proliferation of psychoanalytic theories and about the difficulty in selecting between competing theories in the way that he believes natural science does much more successfully. He describes the present situation where there are overlapping and ill-defined psychoanalytic theories, clustered in different schools and followings, with little capacity for resolution of differences, as a Tower of Babel. In this view, Hinshelwood is taking up concerns previously set out in studies of psychoanalytic practice for example by Robert Wallerstein (2005) and David Tuckett (2005). His book proposes a critical procedure by which competing theories can be subjected to decisive empirical test.

Hinshelwood believes that the fundamental critique of psychoanalysis first advanced by Karl Popper (1963) and developed by Adolf Grünbaum (1974, 1993) has never been adequately refuted. He accepts as an essentially valid model of scientific procedure Popper’s ‘hypothetico-deductive method’, originally set out in The Logic of Scientific Discovery in 1935. According to this, scientific theories set out generalisations, or universal laws, which are subjected to the test of empirical falsification through controlled experiments or observations. This model contrasts with the ‘inductive method’ according to which knowledge is advanced through the accumulation of positive evidence for theories, which Popper believed cannot generate scientific knowledge. Popper attacked as ‘pseudo-sciences’ those theoretical systems, notably Marxism and psychoanalysis, which pretended to the status of a science but failed to meet the requirement of testing by empirical falsification.1

Author biographies

Stella Acquarone, PhD, is an adult and child psychoanalytic psychotherapist and founder of the Parent Infant Clinic and School of Infant Mental Health in 1990 and of the International Pre-Autistic Network (an international charity registered in the UK). Based in London, she has worked for 32 years with parents and infants in the NHS as well as privately, pioneering and laying the foundations of parent-infant psychotherapy. She has presented workshops and conferences and trained professionals all over the world and has published many papers and several books, including Infant–Parent Psychotherapy: A Handbook for Professionals, Signs of Autism in Infants: Recognition and Early Intervention and Upalala: Helping the Helpers. She has been researching and working with infants with special needs and autistic tendencies since 1980, and her ReStart Special Child Focus programme offers an intensive early-intervention treatment approach administered by a multidisciplinary therapy team and based in psychoanalytic thinking.

Catalina Bronstein is a training and supervising analyst of the British Institute of Psychoanalysis and a member of the Association of Child Psychotherapists. She is an adult and child and adolescent psychoanalyst. She studied medicine and psychiatry in Buenos Aires, Argentina. She later trained as a child psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic, London and as a psychoanalyst at the British Institute of Psychoanalysis. She is Visiting Professor at the Psychoanalysis Unit, University College London and was the former London Editor of the International Journal of Psychoanalysis. She has published many papers and chapters and edited the book Kleinian Theory, A Contemporary Perspective. She works privately with adults and adolescents and since 1987 she has worked at the Brent Centre for Adolescents. She is currently editing a book on psychosomatics.

Joshua Durban is a training child and adult psychoanalyst at the Israeli Psychoanalytic Society, Jerusalem, where he also teaches. He is a staff member at the programme of psychotherapy, Sackler School of Medicine, Tel-Aviv University, the post-graduate stream for advanced Kleinian studies. He works in private practice with a special interest in the psychoanalysis of ASD children and adolescents.

Clinical material

Background

Max suffered anoxia during his mother’s labour, which left him with hemiplegic cerebral palsy that affects his right side limbs causing minor but obvious spasticity, some weakness in strength and stamina, and regular pain. Max’s family, which includes his mother, father and older brother Miles (14), understands that the long-term prognosis for Max is uncertain, as ordinary growth across the adolescent years can bring improvement or deterioration. He has access to a wheelchair, which he can use when fatigued, but has never come to his sessions using it.

Max was referred to the local CAMHS clinic when he was almost 10 years old for ‘anger issues’ that included aggressive outbursts in which he physically attacked his mother and destroyed his own valued objects such as the controller for his PlayStation®. Following these explosions he would be very tearful and apologetic, and miserably retreat to his bedroom as though punishing himself with deliberate isolation. He could give no reason for how he felt or behaved. His parents’ attitude to these episodes was telling: they understood his outbursts to communicate that he was in great distress but could genuinely think of nothing that he might be distressed about. In the initial appointment with both parents they were willing and able to acknowledge their son’s disabilities but always in a context of determined positivity, for instance, “He’s been so lucky to get that marvellous customised wheelchair, we’ve been telling him it’s a great piece of kit and all the other kids will be jealous!” They requested individual therapy for Max, hoping someone could “unlock the puzzle” of his unhappiness, and both they and Max reported that he had benefitted from play therapy sessions with a school counsellor but that these had finished unexpectedly when that therapist moved on. On discussing the referral following the meeting with his parents, the CAMHS team agreed to Max being put forward for weekly psychotherapy, but only if this was accompanied by fortnightly sessions for both parents to help them explore and tolerate the reality of their son’s emotional life, including the ongoing loss and pain of having the bad luck to be born with an impairment of this kind, and the anxiety of not knowing how disabled he might be as an adult. Both interventions began when Max was 10 years and four months and continued until the end of his first year in secondary school when he had just turned 12.

Cathy Troupp   Email: cathytroupp@gmail.com

This is a moving account of attempts to help Max, a 10-year-old boy, come to terms with his hemiplegic cerebral palsy and its impact on his life as it unfolds - or at least to help him to bear his pain about it a little. The first presented session is the third assessment session, and it seems that the therapist had already made a warm engagement with Max in the first two assessment sessions, as Max easily acknowledged his wish to continue to come for treatment.

As requested, I will focus particularly on the use of the Goal-based Outcome Measure (GBOM) at the start of treatment and at the six-month review, and the related communication between Max and his therapist.

The therapist introduced the GBOM at the end of the assessment, in the third session, in accordance with the guidance from Law (2009). This guidance also gives advice on the collaborative working up of goals, with therapist and young person as equal contributors with diverse tasks. The therapist’s role is to scaffold and help articulate the young person’s concerns into realistic goals for change, not least because young people often cannot imagine how things could change, or that they could change.

However, in the session reported, the therapist stopped at allowing Max to write down sentences briefly capturing how he felt, without the crucial envisaging of change. From my reading of the material it seemed that the clinical difficulty here, which bedevilled the attempt to use a patient reported outcome measure, was that the therapist her/himself was still in the early stages of helping Max put into words his feelings about his cerebral palsy, be they his fears, his hopes, or his despair. This tentativeness hampered the therapist to such a degree that s/he miscommunicated and inadvertently gave Max the impression that they could set as a goal the removal of his disability altogether. It makes for painful reading to see his hopes briefly raised, then dashed. If the therapist needed more time before setting goals, this would be entirely commensurate with the flexible approach of the GBOM. It is, after all, a clinical tool, and there is no science to the recommendation to set goals by the third session, just clinical utility.

[[RunningHead]]

Marion Milner: the life; Bothered by alligators

Rebecca Bergese

Rebecca Bergese

London
SE13 5ELL
UK

Rebecca Bergese   *Email rebeccabergese@yahoo.co.uk

Marion Milner was an extraordinary person by most standards. An idiosyncratic and imaginative woman, her work and writing have subtly influenced many psychoanalytic practitioners and writers in the decades since she began her clinical supervision and her writing after the second war. A psychoanalyst and an artist she was intrigued by the power of the unconscious mind to influence the external world. For Marion Milner, the professional life of the clinician provided rich opportunities for the study of the unconscious in our lives and to explore the nature of its expression through our conscious activity and feeling.

Emma Letley’s new biography of Marion Milner is a thorough and detailed account of Milner’s work, written by a scrupulous researcher and affectionate devotee. Starting with the details of Milner’s early life and her family history, the biography moves on to provide a chronology of the key events of her life, interwoven with the development of her interests and ideas and her career path. The writing reacquaints us with this original and unusual thinker, opening a door again to a tenacious, energetic and vivacious mind.

Milner grew up in a comfortable and conventional Edwardian household, the youngest child of three. She knew of the struggles and the insecurities that can accompany childhood, brought up by a disappointed, perhaps depressed, mother and a father whose mental frailty affected the whole family. Despite this, Milner enjoyed a happy, sympathetic connection with her father, finding companionship in their shared love of drawing and nature study. At an early age Milner learnt to observe carefully and precisely, recording her observations in sketches and notes alongside her father who found great solace in the countryside around their home. A love of the natural world and its spiritual meaning remained central to Milner throughout her life. She found it always a reliable, meditative space and a source of renewal. Her carefully kept notebooks, sketchbooks and journals became the fundamental tools from which she extracted her thoughts, ideas and paintings throughout the rest of her long life.

[[RunningHead]]

Clinical material

Background

Lizzie was diagnosed with autism at age two and a half and referred for psychotherapy by an independent specialist child psychotherapist following an intensive intervention with her and her family when she was just three. During their own fortnightly sessions with a psychotherapist, Lizzie’s parents regularly returned to the traumatic experience of having watched powerless as Lizzie, having met all her developmental milestones at 18 months, then began to ‘lose’ sociability, humour, interest and eye contact for reasons that remain uncertain. Whilst their other daughter Jane, four years older, went from strength to strength both cognitively and socially, Lizzie, aged three and a half at the start of treatment, had no words, no signs, could not bear to see anyone eat or to sit at a table with food and could not be potty-trained. More painfully still, she no longer seemed to recognise or enjoy her parents except for the functions they could perform for her, pulling their hand towards the fridge if she wanted a drink or towards the door if she wanted to leave. Significantly Lizzie appears to have an ongoing digestive problem that causes stomach or bowel pain, which she feels severely, plus serious allergic skin reactions to certain foods, so that both parents and professionals have wondered whether overwhelming pain associated with the mouth and ‘insides’ is implicated in generating her autism. Lizzie is a thin, blonde girl with a dreamy, slightly pained resting expression.

First month of on-going treatment, Lizzie aged three years, six months

When I come to the waiting room, Dad sees me and calls to Lizzie, who at once starts running the other way. Dad quickly catches up with her and easily turns her back to face me. I crouch down and say, “Hi” to Lizzie, who does not acknowledge or look at me, but runs straight past.

Dad gives Lizzie her soft toy ‘Barbar’, picks her up and carries her down the hallway towards our room. I say to Lizzie, “You’ve brought Barbar”; she shows no sign she has heard. When we get to the lobby, Dad puts his daughter down and again she immediately sprints away from the room and towards some chairs in front of a window. This is done impulsively, like a bird instinctively flying towards the light and away from people but without any notional ‘catch me if you can’ game playing. Dad again retrieves her and physically steers her into the room with a bit of coaxing, saying nervously, “I should probably leave right away?” and asking if he should wait just outside or back in the waiting room. I suggest the waiting room. He sets down Lizzie’s feeder cup on the table and tells her it’s there. Lizzie glances at Dad as he leaves, but otherwise seems unconcerned.

Editorial

Teresa Bailey and Kate Stratton

Kate Stratton

Kate Stratton  

This first edition of the Journal of 2014 is a general one. It opens with another rich and thought-provoking paper by Graham Music in which he tries to demonstrate how psychoanalytic thinking can be combined not only with neurobiological research but also with recent understandings about executive functions. He links neuroscience with Freud’s theories about the ego. Music uses a detailed clinical case to show how important it is to work at the appropriate developmental level of a child where serious cognitive and emotional deficits, resulting from abuse and/or neglect, hamper the child’s most basic abilities to think. The combination of Music’s thoughtful analysis of therapy with a maltreated, developmentally compromised child earlier in his career and his present exceptional capacity to apply and communicate complex neuroscience to this work makes the article a real pleasure to read.

Music’s paper is followed by two articles in which research findings, as part of a professional doctorate in Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy are presented. Amanda Keenan’s examines the impact of unresolved mourning on the adolescent development process after the death of a parent earlier in adolescence. Keenan uses a single case study to describe the themes that emerged and describes how these themes changed over the course of intensive psychotherapy.

Nick Sanderson’s article explores children’s responses to failed gratification. Sanderson puts forward the idea of two separate object relations positions in the face of such failure: schizoid and depressive. He uses process notes from training cases to produce a combination of clinical and theoretical research, demonstrating how the research was undertaken and presenting the findings. A content analysis is used to collect quantitative data about a child’s various responses to failures of gratification.

Gvion and Bar explore the presence of parents during the process of therapy both as supporters of the process and as reminders of the inner and outer reality of the child’s world. Two clinical examples illustrate the complex relationships involved in the therapeutic parent–child–therapist triangle and the impact of the internal and external reality of the parent–child relationship on the therapeutic process.

Psychotic and non-psychotic perceptions of reality

Janet Shaw

Janet Shaw

Leeds
UK

Janet Shaw   *Email: hssjs@leeds.ac.uk
psychosis, Bion, preconception, conceptual development, Matte Blanco, symmetrical thinking

This paper explores the difference between psychotic and non-psychotic perceptions of reality. It begins by outlining the construction of a conceptual framework in infancy. The core of this enables differentiation between self and object, and internal and external space, underlying a non-psychotic perception of reality. The conceptual framework may be inadequately formed or subjected to internal dismantling, in which case a psychotic perception of reality dominates. Case material from two child psychotherapy patients is presented and linked with Bion’s theories of psychosis to illustrate a shift between non-psychotic and psychotic thinking in the analytic hour. A psychotic perception of reality dominated by unconscious processes, as identified by Freud and developed by Matte Blanco, is explored.

Heather Lee-Messner and Elizabeth Stevenson

Elizabeth Stevenson

London
UK

Elizabeth Stevenson  

looked-after children, group work, networks, losses, re-integration, projection, containment

This paper describes group work with five siblings aged between three and nine. They were taken into care following severe abuse involving neglect, physical and emotional abuse. In it, we consider the impact of the losses on the network and the children. We explore how Freud, in his paper ‘Mourning and melancholia’ (1917), and others who built on his work, helped us understand the children’s losses. The sibling group was planned in order to address the children’s need to say goodbye to their birth parents, their foster carers and to each other and to prepare them for their individual separate adoptions. The group ran for 18 months and ended when four children had been placed in their adoptive homes; the last child to be adopted was then seen individually until she was also placed. The group work is described with the use of quotes from sessional material to illuminate the processes for these children in facing their complicated and ambivalent losses, the mourning process and their progress towards becoming individuals in their own right rather than enacting fragmented functional parts/roles on behalf of their sibling group as a whole. Their mourning of the loss of each other was complicated by their earlier reliance on each other to manage the difficulties they had faced when surviving their abusive early lives together.

Short-term psychoanalytic child therapy for anxious children: a pilot study

Tanja Göttken, Lars O. White, Annette M. Klein and Kai von Klitzing Psychotherapy, American Psychological Association, 2014, Volume 51 (1): 148–58

Background: Few studies report treatment outcome for early childhood internalising disorders following psychotherapy, especially psychodynamic techniques. We aimed to investigate effectiveness of a novel, developmentally appropriate, short-term psychodynamic treatment programme for 4- to 10-year-olds with anxiety disorders in an outpatient setting. We conducted a quasi-experimental wait-list controlled study. Thirty children (12 females) with Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV), anxiety disorders and their families received 20–25 sessions of manualised short-term Psychoanalytic Child Therapy (PaCT). We assessed outcome with standardised diagnostic interviews and parent reports of internalising and total problems at all time points. Child puppet interviews and teacher reports were also available for pre–post treatment and follow-up analyses. While 18 families entered treatment immediately, 12 families were first wait-listed before receiving treatment. Analyses of symptom improvement were based on comparisons between groups (treatment vs. wait-list) as well as pre–post and 6-month follow-up data across all families (including wait-listed families). Among the 27 completers, 66.67% (n = 18) no longer met criteria for any anxiety disorder (59.88% in intent-to-treat analysis) while no children remitted across the wait-list interval. Parent-reported child internalising and total problems significantly declined during treatment relative to wait-list. The paper describes the genesis, construction and preliminary reliability testing of the Parent−Infant Relational Assessment Tool (PIRAT). PIRAT is a clinical assessment tool for the identification of risk in the early parent−infant relationship. The rationale was to design a flexible, reliable measure that would enable professionals working with infants and their caregivers to assess the parent−infant relationship as it appears in the consulting room, clinic or home environment and to pinpoint areas of concern at the earliest possible opportunity. The measure was developed in the Parent–Infant Project at the Anna Freud Centre and a subsequent study was undertaken to establish whether it could be successfully transferred to healthcare professionals for use in their workplace settings. A reliability study was conducted with a panel of health professionals, including midwives, health visitors, child protection social workers and clinical psychologists, using videotapes of their consultations in the home or clinic with mothers and infants of 0−2 years old. Verbatim excerpts from the training sessions are included to elucidate the process of training and the ways in which participants engaged with and embedded the measure into their practice.

The paper describes research on children’s responses to failures of gratification. Although this has always been an important area of consideration in psychoanalytic thinking, arguments are put forward for the child’s actual feelings of disappointment being significant in ways that have yet to be fully realised theoretically and clinically within Kleinian object relations. Since Freud first used the term ‘frustration’, it has been applied in psychoanalysis as a means by which to describe in an undifferentiated way all those responses to failures of gratification that have an aggressive content. It will be argued that, in a context of the historical shift in thinking from drive to relational models, there is now perhaps scope to posit the existence instead of two discrete object relational positions towards such failures of aim – that frustrated responses can be differentiated in important structural and developmental ways from disappointed ones, by suggesting that the former are schizoid, whilst the latter are depressive in quality. To try and begin to test the hypothesis that there might be an object relational distinction between feelings of frustration and feelings of disappointment, selected process notes from two training cases became the subject of a combined piece of clinical and theoretical research. I will outline how this research was undertaken and present the findings that arose from the clinical part of it. With the use of a content analysis, a method for gathering interesting quantitative data about the children’s various responses to the failures of gratification was arrived at.

The parental presence as therapy agents, namely as a medium and support for the therapeutic process, is one of the paradoxical parameters of working with children. Parental presence serves as a reminder of the need to find a balance between inner and outer reality. The door that is closed in the therapy room leaves a parent on the other side but at the same time provides the child’s inner world with more latitude to reveal itself. This paper examines the fabric of relations created in the therapeutic parent–child–therapist triangle (analogous to Britton’s conceptualisation of the parent–parent–child link). How does this triangular connection affect the ability to be with the silent self (Winnicott) when the parent remains (tangibly and symbolically) on the other side of the therapy door? This paper presents two clinical examples to illustrate the complex fabric of relations created in the therapeutic parent–child–therapist triangle and the interactions between the internal and external reality of the parent–child relationship.

The paper explores initial, impulsive self-cutting in adolescence and conceives of early cutting as having the most potential for a communicative function, as the adolescents themselves and those around them may be most shocked at their self-harm. The author also conceives of the symptom of early, initial cutting as an effort to ‘cut through’ an emotional and familial circumstance that has been silent, suggesting that cutting generally implies a failure in containment and symbolisation. Using Green’s (1975) discussion of the original word symbol as ‘an object cut in two, constituting a sign of recognition when those who carry it can assemble the two pieces’ (Dictionnaires Le Robert), the author demonstrates that cutting has the potential to elicit intense feelings in the analyst who can have (in Green’s terms) a homologous experience to that of the patient. This elaboration within the analyst’s feelings returns a part to the patient. The meeting of the two communications (the patient’s cutting and the elaboration in the analyst’s mind) can create a potential space between them. The paper uses clinical vignettes and extended clinical material from a 16-year-old girl to elucidate the relationship between cutting – an emotionally inarticulate state – and the development of communication, containment and symbolisation through homologous experiences in the analyst.

Stephen Parker, Professor of Psychology and himself a Wesleyan Methodist, sets out in this book to illustrate the pervasive influence of this particular religious doctrine on Winnicott’s clinical thinking throughout his life, as well as tracing the development of Winnicott’s religious belief under the influence of his growing psychoanalytic insights. Because of the parallels between the religious background of author and subject, the book at times reads like an intense and very specific personal ‘soul searching’ for points of connection and integration between psychoanalytic theory and Wesleyan Methodism – a nonconformist branch of Christianity that emphasises the importance of ethical action springing from a love of humanity. Whilst this narrow and idiosyncratic focus in itself might be of somewhat limited interest or relevance to the general reader, I found this book interesting for the wider questions it raises and explores around the compatibility between psychoanalytic theory and religious belief. Parker contrasts what he sees as Winnicott’s ‘implicitly theological’ stance with Freud’s categorical rejection of religious belief as a pathological defence.

Parker’s highly detailed examination of Winnicott’s family history and background in relation to the development of his clinical thinking brings the clinician to life as a complex and possibly quite conflicted man with a strong capacity for preserving his personal integrity and autonomy of thought, even in the face of public pressure and criticism. Refreshingly, Parker’s book does not shy away from taking a constructively critical stance towards some more problematic aspects of Winnicott’s professional attitude and behaviour – especially his lack of rigour and clarity at times in elaborating his theories and in acknowledging his sources, which possibly points to a certain degree of unresolved narcissism. This issue is hinted at in Chapter 9, which, somewhat alarmingly, discusses Winnicott’s identification as a clinician with a Christ-like saviour figure.

The baby as subject: clinical studies in infant–parent therapy

Michela Biseo

Michela Biseo

London

Michela Biseo   *Email: michela.biseo@annafreud.org

This book will be of interest to those child psychotherapists, infant mental health practitioners and other professionals who work therapeutically with parents, infants and toddlers. Babies should be seen as ‘a person in their own right’ (p. 11). This is the core belief and professional ethos in this book. The editors have gathered contributions from their team and colleagues in the Royal Children’s Hospital Infant Mental Health Programme (IMHP) in Melbourne, Australia to elaborate on the theme of ‘baby as subject’.

The babies who are seen by these clinicians, no matter how small or sick, are kept in the forefront of the clinician’s mind, spoken directly to and treated as the ‘subject’. Facilitating an authentic, live therapeutic encounter is what unites the clinicians’ approaches and work. The different voices, traditions, modalities and settings of more than a dozen multi-disciplinary professionals have made their unique contributions to this book. Many of the authors and practitioners have trained and worked in this method as it has been developed in the RCH IMHP and have taken this model out to their settings such as in GP practices and community clinics. The culture, diversity and size of Australia are also touched on and contextualise the work outlined here.

Therapeutic thought and work is richly detailed in many chapters of careful, moving, sometimes sad and yet finally hopeful encounters. This pioneering multi-disciplinary team work model and approach deserves to be more widely read and disseminated. It will still be considered innovative in many community or CAMHS settings where babies are often not thought about in this close, attentive way. It is even more striking that this model and approach has been possible in a busy paediatric hospital, where the physical–medical needs of sick infants are, by necessity, of the highest priority.

Frances Salo introduces the method by explaining how the therapist will attempt to provide the baby with psychological holding, thus providing an experience of a ‘mind that is available to help contain and process their feelings’ (p. 11). The therapist will communicate with the baby as a person in their own right and may provide an opportunity for the infant to experience a pleasurable playfulness, which helps to develop the infant’s sense of self and joy.

Children who dare too much: child psychotherapy and extreme risk seeking

Fiorenzo Ranieri

Fiorenzo Ranieri

Arezzo
Italy
UF Infanzia e Adolescenza

Fiorenzo Ranieri   *Email: firan@email.it
daredevil children, risk taking, psychic retreats, dissociation, enactment

Extreme risk-seeking behaviours are commonly observed in children. By using observational and clinical material, the precocity of these behaviours is investigated. The author supports the model of an existing connection between the modalities involved in the formation of anticipatory representations and risk-seeking behaviours. The idea that the necessary mental mechanism for anticipating events and predicting risks are formed as early as in the first year of life is also supported. The risk-taker child uses extreme risk seeking as a defensive tool to keep painful emotions out of the way. Every risky action is an attempt to repair those malfunctioning mental mechanisms necessary for the anticipatory process. The development of the capacity for mentalisation during childhood and adolescence enables one to structure more evolved anticipatory mechanisms, progressively less based on action and increasingly more on reflective thought. Children who dare too much or too often are driven by rudimentary or damaged anticipatory mechanisms. The importance of the model for the child psychotherapist working with daredevil children is underlined. Special emphasis is given to dissociation, enactment in the therapeutic relationship and the complex relationship between the psychotherapist and the parents of these risk-seeking young patients.

Young child observation: a development in the theory and method of infant observation

Pamela Sorensen

Pamela Sorensen

Charlottesville
Virginia
USA

Pamela Sorensen   *Email: pbs8c@hotmail.com

One can fall in love with a method. Potters, dancers, monks and mapmakers – all manner of makers and learners strive to acquire the means to explore the part of the 330 universe that draws them. Sometimes, the very method of exploration becomes, in itself, an object of beauty, as it is being practised and applied. Falling in love with a method means experiencing a relationship between discipline and discovery; finding something quite new through one’s own use of means tried and tested before by others and discovering that this allows an encounter with the object of interest in a way that would otherwise be inaccessible. For love to grow, the method must be structured without being rigid. The theory behind the method (and there is always theory behind a method) must serve the object of study, rather than reify it, illuminate rather than designate. In this collection of papers, edited by Simonetta Adamo and Margaret Rustin, we are invited to share in the beauty, vigour and intellectual rigour of the method of Young Child Observation as it is taught at the Tavistock Clinic. Clearly, the contributors to this volume love the method and through it convey the spirit of poet Mary Oliver’s (1992) ‘Instructions for living a life’:

Pay attention.

Be astonished.

Tell about it.

In telling about it, the editors have usefully organised the book into five parts of three or four papers each, with an informative introduction and epilogue that provide historical background and intellectual context for the work of the contributors. Each part can be read separately and in any order, depending on the nature of the reader’s interest.

Part I covers Developmental Issues, focusing on separation, transitions and Oedipal anxieties. Part II offers papers based on observations in the home, bringing to life the child’s growing understanding of the complexities of family life. Part III, Observations in a nursery, shows the profound impact that the culture of the nursery has on the child’s inner world. Part IV, Applications, gives examples of how the method of Young Child Observation can enrich the understanding of workers whose job entails intervention with ill children or those caught up in the social welfare system. Finally, Part V, Research, illustrates how the method may be used to augment and expand quantitative research and deepen the focus on the emotional implications of nursery organisation.

Despair and hope: on some varieties of countertransference and enactment in the psychoanalysis of ASD (autistic spectrum disorder) children

Joshua Durban

Joshua Durban

Tel-Aviv
Israel

Joshua Durban   *Email: j-durban@inter.net.il An earlier version of this article was given at the conference Transference, Countertransference and Enactment Today, University College London, December 2013.
autism, therapeutic despair, hope, countertransference, mantling, child analysis

This article attempts to deal with the feelings of despair and hope in the analyses of autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) children. The analyst’s therapeutic despair and hope might reflect both the child’s split-off and fragmented primitive unconscious phantasies regarding traumatic breakdown, as well as his or her hidden search for reparation. This autistic reparation involves the phantasised acquisition of bodily and mental coverage and containing forms. These phantasies are deposited in the analyst and are manifested in various, sometimes hallucinatory, states of body and mind. The analyst’s ability to move freely between states of despair and hope is thus a crucial factor in maintaining mental space, in reaching for a better understanding of the child and in promoting his development. Using clinical material drawn from two analyses of a young girl and a male adolescent, the article describes the analyst’s countertransference reactions of somatic hallucinations and the phantasies regarding ‘the virtual child’. These represent both the child’s attempts to use the analyst’s mind in order to get rid of catastrophic fears of breakdown and change as well as to convey various means of phantasised autistic reparation and hopes for a benign psychological birth. All these are part of the process of ‘mantling’, in which the child acquires advanced forms of psychic coverage replacing previous autistic objects and autistic sensation shapes. In addition, an attempt is made to differentiate between false and true hope in the process of emergence from autistic encapsulation.

projective identification, transference, psychosomatic, asthma, eczema, dissociation

This article explores the relationship between the development of severe eczema and asthma in an eight-year-old girl and her difficulties with experiencing psychic pain and conflict. The author focuses on the transference dynamics that preceded and surrounded the psychosomatic reaction in the session. The observations in this case may explain why patients, despite feeling taken over by intense physical sensations, can display flatness and superficiality of affect giving the appearance that they are emotionally ‘hollow’. The author proposes that these patients experience an emotional sense of emptiness in themselves and in their objects that is the result of a very early defence of dissociation caused by overwhelming anxieties of annihilation that are lived out in and through the body. The appearance of a psychosomatic symptom during the session can follow the emergence of sudden and intense raw hostile feelings towards the primary object, accompanied by a sense of danger and profound anxiety, as the hated object is also desperately needed for the subject’s own physical/emotional survival. The analyst can contribute to triggering these episodes by failing to contain the patient’s projections, which may lead to the patient feeling forced to re-introject unprocessed and unbearable ‘psycho-physical’ emotions. This article discusses the different degrees – and forms – of symbolic functioning in connection to this girl’s experience of her eczema and asthma and their manifestation in the transference relationship to the therapist.

violence, transference, countertransference, grounded theory, temperature, distance, time, space

The aim of this article is to explore and lend meaning to the role and function of violence in children, in particular boys, who have had disturbing and traumatic early experiences. Psychoanalytic thinking about the role and function of violence, as well as its impact and management in the consulting room, will be central features of this exploration. In a research project involving a single case study, a number of clinical concepts emerged that have potential ramifications for child psychotherapists working with children exhibiting violent and challenging behaviour. The clinical concepts emerged via the application of grounded theory research methodology to clinical data and contribute to the thinking and theory of Meltzer’s use of ‘temperature and distance’ as a means of understanding and regulating emotional states in the therapeutic setting. ‘Time’ and ‘space’ were additional clinical concepts that emerged. These four concepts are considered crucial elements in providing the child psychotherapist with the means to apply transformative and modifying processes to the un-processed and raw externalisation of primitive, violent impulses.

This paper examines how autism may affect the processing and containing of emotions and sensations. At the beginning of life we can hypothesise that the baby develops two means of processing experience: containment that involves a sensory and mimetic trace of relational experience (proto-containment) and containment which, through the α function and projective and introjective functions translates feelings into meaning (♀/♂). Both these means of processing emotional experience remain active throughout life but oscillate the one with the other. The main hypothesis of this work is that the autistic child is not able to oscillate between real containment (♀/♂) and a primitive form of proto-containment. The author aims to explore, through clinical material, the factors which may promote this oscillation. Autistic children often use non-verbal communication. The author examines how a particular type of action can cross the relational void in the therapeutic relationship through a process that can transform feelings of great distress in the analyst via acts that can be described as an Act of Faith, as described by Bion. This form of action that can cross the void is like an artistic performance.

Reading Anna Freud

Edwin Fenn

Edwin Fenn

London
UK

Edwin Fenn   *Email: edwinfenn@yahoo.co.uk

Nick Midgley’s 2013 publication Reading Anna Freud is an easily accessible book that provides an excellent introduction to the numerous writings of Anna Freud, one of the most influential yet also controversial figures in the early days of child analysis. The book sheds light on the development of Anna Freud’s key ideas and her fundamental interest in learning how the lives of children can be improved. Furthermore, 227 the book draws the reader to question the relevance of her pioneering work today; what place do Anna Freud’s ideas have in the history of psychoanalysis? What can her writings teach us now about how to work therapeutically with children? Are her psychoanalytic ideas still relevant to those entrusted with the welfare of infants and young people?

These key questions are the basis of the book and as I continue reading I am presented with a chronology of Anna Freud’s life. I immediately notice that Anna Freud died just before I was born yet her influence on my thinking and that of many psychoanalytic colleagues is profound. It is also evident just how prolific a writer she was. Midgley is, however, clear to state that the intention of his book is not just to provide a biography of Anna Freud, nor does the book seek to provide a full picture of all the contemporary psychoanalytic (or other) ideas that were developing alongside her work but instead intends to introduce the interested reader to the main aspects of Anna Freud’s writing and her key ideas in a number of fields. He does, however, comment on the limited availability of her papers and writings and describes this as a great loss to the psychoanalytic community.

Where he considers appropriate, Midgley does provide some historical and biographical context. This is, however, easily digestible and adds to the liveliness of the book. Indeed, when writing about some of her earliest papers the author conveys a real sense of motion and the beginning of a new movement, supported by direct quotes from Anna Freud; ‘the excitement for opening a whole new field for psychoanalysis was palpable’ (p. 5).
